title: Recent Developments in Inertial and Centrifugal Microfluidic Systems along with the Involved Forces for Cancer Cell Separation: A Review

subsections.content:
Precision oncology has emerged from the broader shift from population-averaged treatment paradigms toward individualized care based on tumor biology, host factors, and evolving disease trajectories. In cancer, this shift is especially urgent because marked interpatient heterogeneity drives variable therapeutic response, toxicity, relapse risk, and survival, even within the same histopathologic subtype. Precision medicine therefore seeks to integrate genomic and non-genomic information into actionable clinical stratification, while AI-enabled analytics are increasingly viewed as complementary tools for extracting clinically useful patterns from complex multimodal datasets ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

This personalized framework has already reshaped cancer therapy through molecular profiling, genotype-informed treatment selection, and adaptive monitoring strategies, particularly in solid tumors such as breast and lung cancer ref [3], ref [6], ref [7]. At the same time, modern immuno-oncology has reinforced the need for better patient-specific biomarkers: although immune checkpoint inhibitors and related immunotherapies have transformed outcomes in several malignancies, response remains highly uneven and can be accompanied by severe immune-related toxicities ref [1], ref [8], ref [9]. These realities motivate technologies that can repeatedly and minimally invasively characterize tumor evolution, treatment sensitivity, and residual disease over time.

Within this context, liquid biopsy has become highly attractive for precision oncology because it can provide serial access to tumor-derived material without the limitations of repeated tissue biopsy. Circulating tumor cells, circulating tumor DNA, and other blood-borne analytes offer opportunities for early detection, prognosis, therapy selection, and longitudinal surveillance of metastasis and treatment resistance ref [10], ref [11], ref [12]. However, the rarity and phenotypic diversity of circulating tumor cells make their isolation technically challenging, creating a strong rationale for high-throughput, label-free microfluidic methods. Inertial and centrifugal microfluidic systems are therefore well positioned at the interface of oncology and engineering, where precise control of microscale forces can support clinically relevant cancer cell separation from complex biofluids ref [13], ref [14], ref [15].

subsections.subsection_title: Scope of This Review and Technical Landscape
subsections.content:
This review focuses specifically on inertial and centrifugal microfluidic systems for cancer-cell separation, with emphasis on force-mediated, label-free operation rather than the broader universe of microfluidic bioanalysis platforms. More general microfluidic and lab-on-a-chip literature established the foundations of integrated fluid handling, microscale transport, and miniaturized analysis that make such separation devices possible, while also highlighting translation challenges in portability, manufacturability, and system integration ref [6], ref [8]. Against that backdrop, our scope centers on platforms that exploit finite-Reynolds-number effects, curvature-induced secondary flow, and geometry-controlled vortices to isolate tumor-associated cells from blood with minimal preprocessing.

Technically, the landscape considered here spans straight inertial channels, spiral and curved channels, contraction-expansion or vortex-based designs, and integrated hybrid chips for circulating tumor cell enrichment. Representative advances include multi-orifice channels that combine inertial lift and vorticity for continuous focusing ref [8], microstructure-induced helical vortices for long-term single-stream focusing ref [12], spiral microchannels with ordered micro-obstacles for enhanced secondary-flow control ref [9], and multimodal inertial architectures that extend separation beyond simple binary cutoffs ref [9]. We also include application-oriented integrated devices for continuous CTC separation from peripheral blood ref [10], because they illustrate how force-based sorting is increasingly embedded within clinically relevant workflows.

Equally important, this review is organized around the involved forces and their interplay across device classes: inertial lift, Dean drag, centrifugal forcing, pressure-driven effects, and near-wall hydrodynamics. Rather than cataloging all cancer microfluidics, we concentrate on how these forces govern focusing, ordering, and size/deformability-based fractionation, where recent reviews of inertial microfluidics and CTC isolation provide essential context for comparing performance, throughput, and translational readiness ref [11], ref [13], ref [14], ref [15].

subsections.subsection_title: Microfluidics as an Enabling Platform for Cancer Research
subsections.content:
Microfluidics has emerged as a foundational platform in cancer research because it offers precise control over microscale transport, cellular organization, and biomechanical cues while using clinically realistic sample volumes. In contrast to conventional 2D culture, microfluidic systems can reconstruct key aspects of the tumor microenvironment—including extracellular matrix architecture, hypoxia, shear stress, interstitial flow, and multicellular crosstalk—in experimentally tractable formats that are better aligned with in vivo tumor biology ref [4], ref [7], ref [8]. This capability is particularly important for studying tumor heterogeneity, invasion, metastasis, and therapy resistance, all of which are strongly shaped by local microenvironmental conditions rather than cancer-cell genotype alone ref [4], ref [9].

A major strength of microfluidics is its convergence with organ-on-a-chip and tumor-on-a-chip technologies. These systems support compartmentalized co-culture, vascular perfusion, and dynamic drug exposure, enabling higher-fidelity models of patient-specific disease states and treatment response than static well-plate assays ref [5], ref [10], ref [11]. Such platforms have been used to model angiogenesis, intravasation/extravasation, and organ-specific metastatic niches, thereby bridging mechanistic cancer biology with preclinical drug development and personalized medicine workflows ref [4], ref [10], ref [12].

Microfluidics also enables single-cell level interrogation, which is crucial given the pronounced functional heterogeneity of tumor and immune populations. Recent advances in microfluidic single-cell cultivation and analysis allow long-term isolation, monitoring, perturbation, and phenotypic profiling of individual cells or small clones, facilitating studies of clonal evolution, rare-cell behavior, and drug susceptibility landscapes ref [6], ref [13], ref [14]. Collectively, these attributes make microfluidics not merely a miniaturized assay format, but an enabling experimental framework that connects cancer modeling, biomarker discovery, and downstream liquid-biopsy-based cell separation technologies central to this review ref [4], ref [5], ref [15].

subsections.subsection_title: Liquid Biopsy and Circulating Tumor Cell Technologies
subsections.content:
Liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive strategy for longitudinal cancer assessment, enabling repeated sampling of tumor-derived analytes from blood for diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and resistance tracking ref [13]. Among these analytes, circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are especially informative because they preserve cellular, morphological, and molecular features of the primary or metastatic lesion, thereby complementing cell-free biomarkers with single-cell level phenotypic and genotypic information ref [13], ref [10]. Yet, their extreme rarity in peripheral blood and marked heterogeneity make enrichment and identification technically demanding, motivating sustained innovation in CTC technologies ref [15], ref [17].

Over the past decade, CTC platforms have diversified from antibody-dependent capture toward hybrid and label-free approaches that exploit size, deformability, electrical response, and hydrodynamic behavior ref [15], ref [17], ref [10]. Immunoaffinity systems remain important for specificity, including micro/nanostructure-enhanced devices and magnetic-particle-assisted capture on structured channels, which can achieve high recovery and enable downstream release of viable cells, but they may miss subpopulations with low or variable EpCAM expression ref [16], ref [9]. This limitation is especially relevant for cells undergoing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and has accelerated interest in physical and label-free enrichment strategies ref [17], ref [10].

Microfluidics has become central to this transition because it enables precise force control, rare-cell handling, and integration of enrichment with on-chip staining, imaging, or collection. Representative examples include low-shear inertial systems for label-free cancer cell isolation from whole blood, biophysical platforms combining vortex enrichment with deformability-based identification, and centrifugal lab-on-a-disc devices that perform rapid size-selective isolation with reduced peripheral instrumentation ref [12], ref [10], ref [19]. Collectively, these developments define the technical backdrop of this review: a shift from purely biomarker-driven CTC capture toward scalable inertial and centrifugal microfluidic workflows that seek high throughput, viability preservation, and compatibility with downstream precision-oncology analyses ref [15], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Inertial and Label-Free Microfluidic Separation Principles
subsections.content:
Inertial and label-free microfluidic separation exploits finite fluid inertia in the laminar, intermediate-Reynolds-number regime to drive deterministic cross-stream migration without antibodies or external fields. In straight channels, the dominant mechanism is the balance between shear-gradient lift, which pushes particles away from the channel center, and wall-induced lift, which repels them from the wall; together these forces establish size-dependent equilibrium positions and focusing lengths that scale strongly with particle diameter, channel dimension, and flow rate ref [24], ref [25], ref [27]. Foundational studies further showed that rectangular cross-sections reduce the number of stable focusing positions and enable continuous ordering and separation, establishing the basis for high-throughput, sheath-free operation ref [28], ref [23].

For cancer cell separation, label-free performance arises because tumor cells often differ from hematologic cells in size, shape, and deformability, causing different lift-force balances and migration trajectories. Beyond straight channels, structured geometries intensify or redirect these effects. In spiral microchannels, Dean vortices generated by curvature superimpose a transverse drag on inertial lift, and the resulting lift-to-Dean-drag competition underpins differential migration and continuous size fractionation ref [26], ref [24]. This principle has become central to spiral separators for isolating larger rare cells from smaller blood cells at high throughput ref [26], ref [27].

Contraction-expansion and vortex-based designs extend the same label-free logic by introducing localized secondary flows, abrupt acceleration, and recirculating regions that enhance selectivity or shorten focusing length. Reviews of contraction-expansion systems emphasize how geometry-tailored inertial and secondary-flow fields can improve focusing robustness and separation efficiency ref [12]. Likewise, vortex-aided inertial devices can continuously siphon larger particles or cells into trapping or collection paths with high size selectivity, efficiency, and purity ref [13]. Collectively, these mechanisms make inertial microfluidics a scalable physical sorting framework for CTC-relevant enrichment, especially when biochemical labels are undesirable or unavailable ref [23], ref [27].

subsections.subsection_title: Platform Architectures, Flow Control, and Detection
subsections.content:
Centrifugal microfluidic platforms are architecturally distinguished by their rotor-based integration of chambers, radial channels, and passive or externally addressable valves, enabling pump-free liquid propulsion through the centrifugal pressure field while preserving a compact instrument/disposable-cartridge separation. Early “lab-on-a-CD” concepts established the core design language of reservoir-to-channel networks, capillary and hydrophobic barriers, metering structures, and parallel spoke-like assay layouts ref [29]. This architecture matured into the Bio-Disk paradigm, where coherent libraries of unit operations and standardized rotor formats supported increasingly complex assay automation and better manufacturability in thermoplastics ref [31], ref [34].

Flow control on rotating discs relies on the programmable interplay of centrifugal, capillary, pneumatic, and—in some layouts—Coriolis forces. Beyond classical burst valves and siphons, frequency-programmed routing has been exploited for transversal flow control, where Coriolis effects at elevated angular velocity bias flow in symmetric outlets and permit speed-dependent switching without additional actuators ref [32]. More broadly, advanced centrifugal platforms combine overflow metering, pneumatic energy storage, siphon priming, and passive/active valving to execute multistep protocols with minimal world-to-chip interfacing ref [34]. Active control has also progressed through optically triggered ferrowax microvalves, in which laser-irradiated nanoparticle-loaded wax enables fast, localized, and multifunctional normally-open or normally-closed valve actuation suitable for sequential disc operations ref [33].

Detection on lab-on-a-disc systems is predominantly optical because the rotating cartridge is naturally compatible with transmission, fluorescence, and imaging-based readout. Comprehensive surveys have shown that centrifugal platforms support both stop-and-go and on-the-fly detection modes, including absorbance, fluorescence, chemiluminescence, stroboscopic imaging, and even optical-disc-drive-derived scanning strategies ref [30]. Important engineering advances include beam-guided absorbance paths that extend optical path length on-disc, robust synchronization of imaging with rotation, and adaptation of commercial optical pickup concepts for low-cost readout ref [29], ref [30], ref [31]. Together, these developments make platform architecture, flow control, and detection tightly co-designed elements rather than separable subsystems in contemporary lab-on-a-disc technology ref [34].

Sample preparation on centrifugal microfluidic discs is dominated by blood conditioning, plasma extraction, and pre-analytical cleanup, because downstream molecular or cellular assays are highly sensitive to residual cells, hemolysis, and poorly timed fluid transfer. Early lab-on-disc studies established rapid decanting-based plasma extraction from whole blood, yielding metered plasma volumes with low residual cell contamination and direct compatibility with subsequent on-disc handling ref [39]. Related high-speed architectures further reduced processing time by combining rotationally induced sedimentation with channel-level inertial effects and branching geometries, although performance generally depended on hematocrit and operating speed ref [40].

A major line of development focused on more robust flow control during blood processing. Centrifugo-pneumatic gating enabled stopped-flow sedimentation followed by triggered plasma release without local surface treatment or sacrificial materials, providing efficient plasma recovery with low residual cell counts in a compact footprint ref [37]. Likewise, out-of-plane microvalves improved spatial isolation between supernatant and sedimentation reservoirs, suppressing back-diffusion of blood cells and enabling high plasma purity and yield from whole blood ref [7]. These approaches illustrate how centrifugal, capillary, pneumatic, and hydrostatic forces are co-designed to stabilize interfaces during sample cleanup.

Beyond simple plasma harvesting, rotating discs have also supported richer fractionation and integrated pretreatment. Density-gradient platforms separated microliter-scale whole-blood samples into multiple removable fractions, enabling leukocyte enrichment, direct microscopy, and recovery of viable cells from distinct density bands ref [38]. At the assay-preparation level, fully integrated discs combined plasma separation with magnetic capture, washing, and laser-assisted lysis to extract pathogen-specific DNA from whole blood in a short, minimally manual workflow ref [36]. Such capabilities are directly relevant to cancer diagnostics, where upstream enrichment of plasma, leukocytes, or nucleic acids can condition specimens before rare-cell isolation or liquid-biopsy analysis.

Biochemical analysis on centrifugal microfluidic platforms has progressed from proof-of-concept fluid handling to genuinely integrated assay execution, where metering, mixing, incubation, separation and optical readout are all performed on-disc. Early work demonstrated that centrifugal pumping is sufficiently robust across wide flow-rate ranges and compatible with biological fluids, enabling parallelized enzymatic testing in compact disc formats; notably, 48 simultaneous colorimetric assays were implemented on a single rotor, illustrating the suitability of rotating discs for high-throughput biochemical screening ref [42]. Beyond simple pumping, subsequent systems integrated frequency-programmed valving, rapid mixing, and real-time optical interrogation to shorten assay turnaround while maintaining quantitative performance ref [41].

Detection strategies have likewise diversified. Real-time absorbance measurement with monolithically integrated optical beam guidance enabled whole-blood alcohol analysis directly on-disc, combining nanoliter-scale metering, sedimentation of blood cells, and kinetic extrapolation for rapid colorimetric readout ref [41]. Fluorescence-based sensing further extended analytical capability: ion-selective optode membranes incorporated into rotating platforms supported sequential calibration and quantification of potassium and nitrite, while laser-diode excitation improved sensitivity and supported more compact instrumentation ref [43]. In parallel, array-based bead handling has enabled capture, counting and multiplexed bead assays under highly reproducible stopped-flow sedimentation conditions, simplifying assay readout by arranging particles in a single focal plane ref [45].

At the cellular level, lab-on-a-disc systems have also been adapted for functional analysis rather than merely bulk biochemical measurement. A centrifugal flow disk with aligned microchambers enabled rapid single-cell isolation followed by on-disc cultivation, allowing activity assessment through proliferation of bacterial, yeast, lymphoid and fibroblast cells from initially isolated single cells ref [44]. This capability is important for cancer-related applications because it links centrifugal sample manipulation to downstream phenotypic interrogation, including viability, growth dynamics and potentially drug-response assays at the single-cell level. Collectively, these studies show that rotating-disc platforms support not only sample preparation but also integrated biochemical assays and cellular analytics in formats compatible with decentralized diagnostics ref [41], ref [42], ref [43], ref [44], ref [45].

subsections.subsection_title: Rare-Cell and Tumor-Cell Isolation on Rotating Discs
subsections.content:
Rare-cell isolation on rotating discs has progressed from proof-of-concept enrichment to increasingly automated CTC workflows that integrate capture, purification, and readout on a single platform. Early disc-based systems demonstrated that centrifugal actuation can replace bulky syringe-pump infrastructure while preserving gentle handling of scarce cells, an important feature for downstream characterization ref [48]. In this context, stopped-flow centrifugo-magnetophoretic purification enabled direct immunomagnetic enrichment from whole blood and rapid bright-field enumeration of rare cancer cells, highlighting the value of combining centrifugal sedimentation with lateral magnetic deflection for low-loss recovery and simplified instrumentation ref [48].

Subsequent lab-on-a-disc designs targeted higher throughput and greater clinical utility. An all-in-one membrane-based disc integrated size-selective filtration, washing, staining, and enumeration, allowing label-free CTC isolation from whole blood within seconds of filtration and with substantially reduced leukocyte carryover compared with conventional membrane devices ref [17]. In parallel, a fully automated large-volume platform used bead-assisted density amplification and density-gradient transport on a rotating disc to process up to 5 mL blood, achieving high recovery together with very low leukocyte contamination suitable for mutation analysis ref [46]. These studies illustrate two dominant disc strategies for tumor-cell isolation: size-based capture for simplicity and speed, and affinity-plus-density engineering for higher purity and molecular testing readiness ref [17], ref [46].

More recently, continuous centrifugal microfluidics (CCM) has addressed a key limitation of earlier approaches: bias against phenotypically diverse CTCs. By synchronizing laser-actuated valving with ongoing rotation, CCM enabled precise extraction of the PBMC layer during continuous centrifugation and then performed negative depletion of CD45-positive leukocytes, yielding high recovery across EpCAM-positive, EpCAM-negative, small, large, and clustered CTC populations ref [47]. Clinical studies in EGFR-mutant NSCLC further showed that such rotating-disc systems can recover heterogeneous CTC subsets for enumeration and mutational profiling, supporting their role in liquid-biopsy workflows where automation, throughput, and reduced selection bias are all essential ref [46], ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Force Frameworks Governing Particle Behavior in Microfluidic and Rotational Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Particle Transport in Complex and Biomedical Flow Environments
subsections.content:
Particle transport in biomedical microflows deviates substantially from the behavior predicted for isolated rigid spheres because cells travel in concentrated, multicomponent suspensions with deformability, adhesion, and biochemical cross-talk. In blood, circulating tumor cells (CTCs) experience not only viscous drag and wall interactions, but also repeated encounters with erythrocytes, platelets, leukocytes, fibrin, and endothelial interfaces, which reshape trajectories, residence times, and margination probabilities ref [49], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. Such complexity is especially relevant for liquid-biopsy devices, where the target population is rare and biologically heterogeneous ref [5], ref [6].

A central feature of CTC transport is cooperative shielding by blood constituents. Platelet coating can increase effective hydrodynamic size, alter surface roughness, and promote immune evasion, while platelet-derived signals also enhance epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity and survival against anoikis ref [49], ref [7], ref [8]. Neutrophils and monocytes further contribute through transient aggregates, chemokine-mediated recruitment, and endothelial tethering, thereby facilitating arrest and extravasation; CTC clusters and CTC–leukocyte microemboli are particularly associated with enhanced metastatic competence ref [49], ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. These phenomena imply that separation platforms must handle not only single cells, but also multicellular complexes with time-varying mechanical properties.

From a microfluidic perspective, these biomedical interactions modify the force balance that governs focusing and separation. Deformability, adhesion, and cluster formation shift cells away from ideal size-only scaling, while hematocrit-dependent collisions and near-wall margination can either improve or degrade enrichment depending on channel geometry and shear regime ref [2], ref [5], ref [12]. Consequently, clinically robust inertial and centrifugal systems should be designed around physiologically realistic suspensions, preserving viable transport while exploiting differences in size, stiffness, and interaction propensity between CTCs and hematologic backgrounds ref [6], ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Force Frameworks Governing Particle Behavior in Microfluidic and Rotational Systems
subsections.content:
Microfluidic implementations of focusing forces can be broadly classified into sheath-based and sheathless strategies, with recent emphasis on passive, geometry-enabled focusing that avoids bulky external fields while preserving high throughput. In inertial microfluidics, focusing is realized by exploiting finite-Reynolds-number lift forces together with channel-induced secondary flows, so that particles migrate toward well-defined equilibrium positions determined by channel cross-section, curvature, and particle size ref [25]. These principles are especially attractive for cancer-cell processing because they enable continuous enrichment and pre-alignment before downstream detection or collection.

A representative implementation beyond conventional sheath-flow confinement is the micro-weir microchannel, in which gradually reduced weir heights generate localized shear and a Saffman-type lift contribution that focuses particles simultaneously in the horizontal and vertical directions ref [50]. In that design, 5 and 10 μm beads were reported to pass the detection region in a one-by-one manner with focusing performances exceeding 99%, illustrating how local topographic perturbations can convert shear-lift physics into practical three-dimensional focusing for microflow cytometry ref [50]. Such architectures are noteworthy because they achieve passive alignment without auxiliary sheath streams, electrodes, or acoustic transducers.

More generally, the literature shows that focusing forces are implemented through several recurring channel motifs: straight rectangular channels that exploit wall and shear-gradient lift; spiral channels that superimpose inertial lift with Dean drag; contraction-expansion and multi-orifice channels that introduce localized acceleration and vortex-assisted cross-stream migration; and serpentine or pillar-structured channels that reshape secondary flows to compress particles into one or a few streamlines ref [25]. For biomedical separations, these implementations are not merely fluidic conveniences: they determine whether rare, larger, and often more deformable circulating tumor cells can be preferentially displaced relative to blood cells, thereby coupling hydrodynamic focusing with size- and mechanics-based discrimination ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Force Frameworks Governing Particle Behavior in Microfluidic and Rotational Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Inertial Lift and Particle Migration in Channel Flows
subsections.content:
Inertial lift in channel flow arises from finite-Reynolds-number corrections that break the reversibility of creeping motion and drive particles across streamlines toward discrete equilibrium locations. Classical analyses established that migration reflects a competition between shear-gradient lift, which pushes particles away from the channel center toward regions of higher shear, and wall-induced lift, which repels them from nearby boundaries; their balance explains the Segre–Silberberg effect in Poiseuille flow and its extension to microchannels ref [51], ref [53], ref [23]. For neutrally buoyant particles, this balance yields stable off-center attractors, whereas for particles with slip or buoyancy, additional Saffman-type contributions can shift equilibria toward or away from walls depending on the sign of the slip velocity ref [51], ref [53].

Matched-asymptotic treatments clarified that inertial migration depends not only on particle size and channel Reynolds number, but also on local shear and velocity-profile curvature. In particular, Asmolov showed that at large channel Reynolds number the near-wall force approaches the single-wall linear-shear limit, while in the channel core the wall contribution weakens and curvature remains important, so the lift does not reduce to a purely local linear-shear prediction ref [51]. Experiments in pipe Poiseuille flow further confirmed wallward migration of the classical annulus with increasing Reynolds number and revealed finite-size deviations from point-particle theory, including secondary inner annuli at elevated Reynolds numbers ref [53].

For microfluidic design, these migration laws imply that focusing length decreases strongly with particle size and increases when lift coefficients diminish at higher Reynolds number, making finite-size, aspect-ratio, and entrance-length effects central to device performance ref [52], ref [23]. More recent microchannel studies therefore interpret focusing as a two-stage process: rapid migration from the core to near-wall manifolds dominated by shear-gradient and wall lift, followed by slower drift along walls toward face-centered equilibria, with rotation-induced lift helping explain why rectangular channels can support two or four stable focusing positions depending on aspect ratio and flow conditions ref [23], ref [52]. This framework is directly relevant to cancer-cell separation, where subtle differences in size, deformability, and slip-like behavior alter migration trajectories and final focusing positions.

subsections.section_title: Force Frameworks Governing Particle Behavior in Microfluidic and Rotational Systems
subsections.content:
Classical particle hydrodynamics in microfluidics is rooted in the low-Reynolds-number force balance for rigid spheres, where viscous drag, buoyancy, and pressure-induced stresses set the baseline for particle motion. Stokes’ treatment of viscous resistance established the canonical linear drag law for creeping flow, while subsequent analyses clarified how internal friction and added-fluid effects alter oscillatory and translational motion in real fluids ref [54], ref [4], ref [6]. These ideas remain directly relevant to cell sorting, because many separation platforms operate in regimes where Stokes drag is the first-order predictor of transit speed, sedimentation tendency, and relaxation toward streamlines ref [5], ref [7].

Beyond drag, classical theory also identified important corrections associated with slip, rotation, and confinement. Cunningham showed that very small particles in gases deviate from the no-slip Stokes prediction, motivating the well-known slip correction for terminal settling velocities ref [5]. For rotating particles, Rubinow and Keller derived a transverse lift proportional to the cross product of spin and translational velocity, providing a viscous analogue of Magnus-type behavior at small Reynolds number ref [55]. In bounded suspensions, Faxén and Brenner further demonstrated that nearby walls and flow curvature modify both drag and torque, which is especially pertinent in narrow microchannels and disc-based separators where finite gap effects are unavoidable ref [8], ref [9], ref [10].

These classical force models underpin modern interpretations of cancer-cell handling in microfluidic and centrifugal systems. Density contrast determines centrifugal sedimentation through the same balance underlying terminal fall ref [5], whereas particle size, deformability, and near-wall position perturb the nominal drag/lift response away from ideal rigid-sphere behavior ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. Thus, although contemporary inertial and elasto-inertial devices exploit higher-order migration mechanisms, their design still depends on the classical hydrodynamic framework as the reference state from which biomedical particles, including circulating tumor cells, begin to deviate ref [54], ref [55], ref [14].
